To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability to spread and to form cell sheets is lost by cells of tumorigenically transformed cultures, that this loss is accompanied by a disorganization of the microfilament and microtubule networks in the cytoplasm, and that the distribution of fibronectin is altered.

the ability of the cells to adhere to substratum and to each other is a major feature of the transformed phenotype, and that the cytoskeletal organization in tumorigenic cells differs from that in the parental non-tumorigeneic cells.

the ability of epithelioid cells to spread on the surface is a key characteristic of the epithelial phenotype, and that the loss of this ability is the most common morphological change that accompanies neoplastic transformation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms involved in the transformation of normal cells to malignant ones.
the study of the morphological alterations associated with neoplasia.
the morphological changes associated with the loss of growth control in rat liver cells in culture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes in cell shape and cytoskeleton in the IAR cell lines were not a result of the transformation process per se but a result of the altered cell-cell interactions.
there are no specific cytoskeletal changes that are common to all transformed cells.
the cytoskeleton is not a static structure but rather a dynamic one that changes with time and in response to the external environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in the cyto-architecture of tumorigenic cells may be the result of the loss of the ability of these cells to interact with their normal microenvironment.
the cytoskeletal changes associated with neoplastc transformation are not specific for a particular type of tissue.
the cytoskeleton of transformed cells is altered in a tissue-specific manner, and that the alterations are not limited to changes in the organization of actin microfilaments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cytoskeletal changes in transformed epithelial cells are not identical to those observed in transformed fibroblasts.
cell shape is not a fixed property of a cell type.
